🚀 Caelum Novum – Exploring Beyond Boundaries

We are Caelum Novum, a multidisciplinary team bringing together mathematics, programming, machine learning, and curiosity to tackle challenges inspired by space and science.

Our team combines analytical thinking, software development, AI-driven problem-solving, and fresh perspectives. With a mathematician, a programmer, an ML developer, and an enthusiastic beginner eager to learn and contribute, we believe great ideas emerge when different skills.
summary:
Trend Detective is a prediction tool that turns NASA Earth science data into early warnings of drought and flood risk. Given a state and a measurement, such as soil moisture or precipitation from NASA’s GPM IMERG, FLDAS and NLDAS datasets, it first tests whether the long-term change is statistically significant, using a seasonal Mann-Kendall test that removes the yearly cycle. It then uses that history to estimate the chance that next month will be unusually dry or wet, and shows how much more or less likely that is than normal.

Predictions are validated honestly. Each one is backtested against simply guessing the usual rate, and when it doesn’t beat guessing, the tool says so rather than overclaiming. A 3D terrain map is designed to show where predicted hotspots will occur, and charts and plain-English explanations make the results understandable to non-experts.

This matters because slow environmental changes, like drying soils, raise risks before disasters happen. Anticipating them helps communities, farmers and planners prepare.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
Trend Detective helps anyone find out whether a part of the Earth is really changing. The user chooses a state and a measurement, such as precipitation or soil moisture at four depths. The tool plots the full NASA record, draws the overall trend line and answers four questions in plain English: what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the change is statistically significant. It also estimates the chance of drought-like or flood-prone conditions next month, and shows a 3D terrain map where predicted hotspots appear as glowing markers sized by probability.

HOW IT WORKS
We pull area-averaged monthly data for each state from NASA Giovanni: GPM IMERG precipitation and FLDAS and NLDAS soil moisture. A data pipeline cleans the files and converts everything to everyday units (millimetres of rain per month, percent of soil volume). Trends are tested with a seasonal Mann-Kendall test and Sen’s slope, which compare each calendar month only with the same month in other years, so the yearly cycle cannot create a fake trend. The chance-of-event card uses a historical-frequency model: it looks at how often very dry or very wet months followed months in the same condition, and is backtested against simply guessing the usual rate.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT
NASA’s data is enormous and hard to interpret. We want students, communities and local planners to spot environmental change early, such as a drying trend that raises drought risk, without needing a statistics background. Every result is explained in everyday language with its uncertainty shown.

TOOLS
Python, Flask, pandas and NumPy for the backend and statistics; Plotly for interactive charts; MapLibre GL JS for the 3D terrain map; Bootstrap and GSAP. Data comes from NASA Giovanni. We used ordinary laptops and no special hardware.

WHAT IS CREATIVE
The tool turns statistics into sentences a non-expert can act on. It shows two independent NASA models side by side so users can see whether they agree. It reports its own accuracy honestly: when a prediction does not beat guessing, the tool says “treat with caution” instead of hiding it. We also tested the trend engine on made-up series with known trends to confirm it recovers them and does not raise false alarms.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED
Seasonality hiding trends; records that start or end mid-year; differing units between models (FLDAS and NLDAS report soil water differently, so we converted both to a common unit); short records, which are flagged because they rarely give reliable trends; the difference between “statistically significant” and “large”; and a non-technical audience. The map and hotspot file format are designed so a machine-learning model can plug in later.
